title: The Calloway Family: Integrated Investment Planning Case
stem:
The Calloway family asks a CFP® professional to coordinate their investment plan.

Graham Calloway, 53, operations director at a privately held freight-logistics company (salary $165,000). Nadia Calloway, 50, senior software engineer at Kestrel Diagnostics, Inc., a publicly traded medical-testing company (salary $185,000). Married filing jointly; they itemize deductions. Children: Leah, 15 (starts college in three years) and Sam, 11. Both are in good health and carry adequate life, disability and umbrella coverage. Assume today is January 1 of the current year.

Goals

  • Hold a cash reserve equal to six months of living expenses.
  • Have Leah’s first-year college money available in three years.
  • Both retire in about 12 years (Graham at 65, Nadia at 62).
  • Reduce reliance on Kestrel stock without a large immediate tax bill.
  • Keep investment costs and taxes low.

Risk profile

  • Joint questionnaire score: moderate.
  • Graham sold most of his stock funds near the bottom of a past bear market and says a 15% drop would cost him sleep.
  • Nadia is comfortable with volatility and would like an actively managed sleeve in emerging markets and REITs.
  • Graham prefers low-cost index funds and little trading.

items.q: In which section of the Calloways' investment policy statement (IPS) should these two needs be recorded?
o: Return requirement
Liquidity
Laws and regulations
Permitted and excluded investments
items.e: Liquidity constraints record money the clients must be able to reach: an emergency reserve and any known outlay within roughly the next three to five years, such as tuition. Many advisors keep money needed inside five years out of the stock market. The return requirement states the target return; laws and regulations mainly concern plans like ERISA trusts; permitted/excluded investments lists the clients’ preferences.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Calloways' risk tolerance for the IPS?
o: Low ability and low willingness; the IPS should target capital preservation and leave the 6.5% goal as is
High ability and high willingness; their net worth lets the IPS set above-average volatility
Low ability but high willingness; the planner should rely on the questionnaire score alone
High ability but low willingness; the IPS should record both and reconcile the risk level with the 6.5% requirement
items.e: Ability depends on resources and circumstances (wealth, income, insurance, horizon), and the Calloways’ is high. Willingness is emotional comfort with swings, and Graham’s history shows it is low. The IPS addresses both, and the risk objective must fit the return requirement: if 6.5% needs more risk than they will accept, they must accept more risk, lower the goal, or do some of each.

items.q: How large is the gap in the Calloways' emergency reserve, and what is the best way to close it?
o: $19,000; add it to a money market holding from the cash-flow surplus or taxable assets
$19,000; arrange a 401(k) loan that can be drawn if an emergency occurs
$81,000; open a home equity line of credit to serve as the whole reserve
$39,000; leave the CD out of the reserve and draw the gap from the 401(k)s
items.e: Target = 6 × $13,500 = $81,000. Liquid assets = $18,000 + $24,000 + $20,000 = $62,000. Gap = $81,000 − $62,000 = $19,000. The reserve belongs in highly liquid, marketable holdings such as a money market account so short-term setbacks never force a sale of long-term assets or new borrowing. Their $47,600 surplus can fill the gap within the year.

items.q: Which response by the planner is most accurate?
o: She is right; both accounts carry FDIC coverage up to $250,000 per ownership category
She is right only if the fund holds Treasury bills, which makes the fund itself FDIC insured
The mutual fund is not federally insured; a bank money market deposit account is insured up to $250,000 per ownership category
Neither account is insured, but only the bank account permits check-writing
items.e: Money market mutual funds are offered by open-end investment companies and are not federally insured, although they hold high-quality short-term paper and are very liquid. A money market deposit account (MMDA) is a bank obligation insured up to $250,000 per ownership category (2026 edition figure). Either can hold an emergency fund; the client simply needs to know the difference.

items.q: What is the Calloways' after-tax, inflation-adjusted return on the T-bills?
o: −0.27%
−0.47%
items.e: T-bill interest is federally taxed but state-exempt, so use 32% only (2026 edition figure). After-tax = 4.0% × (1 − 0.32) = 2.72%. Real = [(1.0272 ÷ 1.03) − 1] × 100 = −0.27%. The roll-over keeps reserve money safe but loses purchasing power: fine for an emergency fund, a poor home for long-term money.

items.q: What is the planner's best course of action with Graham?
o: Keep a long-term perspective and hold the IPS allocation, reminding Graham why it was chosen
Move the 401(k) to stable value now and re-enter after the market regains half its loss
Shift half the 401(k) to stable value as a compromise to ease Graham’s anxiety
Rewrite the IPS around capital preservation because a 25% decline changes their goals
items.e: With jobs, reserves and a 12-year horizon intact, the decline is market turmoil, not a change in the clients’ own situation. When a client presses to move to cash, the best course is usually no action: keep the allocation and the long view. Markets carry a long-term positive bias that rewards patient, diversified investors; abandoning the plan tends to leave clients on the sidelines early in a recovery.

items.q: Which event(s) should prompt the planner to reassess the assumptions in the Calloways' IPS?
o: I and III
II and III
III only
I, II, and III
items.e: Change comes in three kinds. Noise (II) carries no meaning and is ignored. Incremental change (I) is a small extension of an existing pattern and bears watching. Discontinuous change (III), such as losing a job, is a radical break that calls for revisiting the IPS assumptions: income, liquidity, risk capacity and the Kestrel holding.

items.q: Which approach best reconciles the spouses' preferences for their retirement assets?
o: Tactical asset allocation applied to the entire portfolio
A single moderate model portfolio from a fund sponsor’s questionnaire
A strategic allocation held entirely in index funds with no active component
A core-and-satellite strategy: a passive index core plus a smaller active satellite sleeve
items.e: Core and satellite puts most assets in passive broad-market index funds (the core, run strategically) and a smaller share in higher-risk opportunities such as emerging markets, REITs or high-yield bonds (the satellite, run tactically). Its aims (diversification, returns in line with the required return, low transaction costs, tax management) fit both spouses.

items.q: Which strategy best meets Nadia's goals for her Kestrel shares?
o: Contribute the shares to an exchange fund
Transfer the shares to a charitable remainder trust
Give the shares to Leah and Sam
Sell the shares and buy a diversified index fund
items.e: An exchange fund takes concentrated public stock in return for a proportional interest in a diversified pool, spreading the company-specific (unsystematic) risk without an immediate capital gains tax, and Nadia keeps the value. A CRT avoids tax on the sale but leaves the remainder to charity; gifting gives up ownership; an outright sale taxes the $200,000 gain (4,000 × $50).

items.q: Ignoring commissions, what is the minimum net value of Nadia's hedged KDX position at expiration (the value the puts lock in, less the premium paid)?
items.e: Premium = 40 contracts × 100 × $2.50 = $10,000. However far KDX falls, she can sell at $80: 4,000 × $80 = $320,000. Net floor = $320,000 − $10,000 = $310,000, versus $360,000 today. A protective put works like insurance: she keeps the upside, but the cost recurs and coverage ends at expiration.

items.q: Which option position should Nadia add to her 4,000 KDX shares?
o: Buy 40 $80 puts and write 40 $105 calls with offsetting premiums
Write 40 $105 covered calls and nothing else
Write 40 $80 puts and buy 40 $105 calls
Buy 40 $90 calls and 40 $90 puts (a long straddle)
items.e: A zero-cost collar = long stock + long put + short call. The $80 put sets a floor; the premium received for the $105 call pays for the put, so the net cost is about zero. The trade-off: shares may be called away above $105. Covered calls alone cap the upside but give only premium-sized protection in a sharp drop.

items.q: Using the CAPM, what is the required return on KDX, and what does it imply about adding to the position?
o: 18.0%; KDX is undervalued, so buy more
12.4%; the expected return falls short, so do not add to KDX
8.4%; the expected return exceeds it, so add to KDX
14.0%; KDX plots on the security market line, so hold it unchanged
items.e: CAPM: r = r<sub>f</sub> + (r<sub>m</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>)β = 4.0% + (10.0% − 4.0%)(1.40) = 4.0% + 8.4% = 12.4%. The 11.0% expected return is below the 12.4% required, so KDX plots below the SML (priced too high for its systematic risk) and the CAPM test says reject further purchases. It supports the diversification plan.

items.q: What is the weighted beta of the equity holdings in the joint brokerage account?
items.e: Weighted beta = Σ(value × beta) ÷ total value = ($504,000 + $97,750 + $33,354) ÷ $482,060 = $635,104 ÷ $482,060 = 1.32. The sleeve is about 32% more volatile than the market. With one stock at 75% of it, beta understates total risk, because company-specific risk has not been diversified away.

items.q: Using the R² threshold taught in the course, which fund is the effective diversifier for Graham's account?
o: Large-Cap Value Index, R² = 0.88
Mid-Cap Blend, R² = 0.79
International Developed Index, R² = 0.38
Dividend Growth, R² = 0.74
items.e: R² = R × R. Morningstar treats an R² above 70% (correlation above about 0.84) as too tied to the market to diversify an S&P 500 holding. Only the international fund (0.62² = 0.38) is under 70%; most of its movement comes from factors other than the S&P 500. A low positive correlation is enough; a negative one is not required.

items.q: Which fund shows the better risk-adjusted performance, using the appropriate measure?
o: Bexley, because its Treynor ratio (7.50) beats Alder’s (7.24)
Bexley, because its return is 1.4 points higher than Alder’s
Alder, because its higher R² shows it has the better manager
Alder, because its Sharpe ratio (0.48) beats Bexley’s (0.41)
items.e: Bexley’s R² of 0.58 is below 0.70, so its beta is unreliable and beta-based measures (Treynor, Jensen) are suspect. Use Sharpe = (R<sub>p</sub> − R<sub>f</sub>) ÷ σ. Alder: (11.6 − 4.0) ÷ 16.0 = 0.48. Bexley: (13.0 − 4.0) ÷ 22.0 = 0.41. Alder delivers more excess return per unit of total risk.

items.q: Which of these statements about Harborline are CORRECT? I. Its high turnover adds trading costs not included in the 1.25% expense ratio. II. Its high turnover can produce capital gains distributions taxable to the Calloways. III. The expense ratio already includes the fund's brokerage commissions. IV. The manager's departure is a reason to monitor the fund more closely.
o: I and III
II and IV
I, II, and IV
I, II, III, and IV
items.e: Turnover generates commissions, bid-ask spreads and market-impact costs, none of which appear in the expense ratio (I true; III false, since the ratio covers operating expenses, management fees and 12b-1 fees). High turnover can also realize gains that are distributed and taxed in a taxable account (II). Losing the manager behind the record calls for closer monitoring, though weaker results are not certain (IV).

items.q: What loss can the Calloways recognize on the December sale, and what is their basis in the repurchased shares?
o: $0 loss; basis $97,000
$0 loss; basis $82,000
items.e: Buying the same security within 30 days before or after selling it at a loss (2026 edition figure) is a wash sale. The $15,000 loss ($85,000 − $100,000) is postponed, not lost: it is added to the new shares’ basis, $82,000 + $15,000 = $97,000. Waiting more than 30 days to buy Harborline back would have kept the loss deductible.

items.q: What is the municipal fund's taxable-equivalent yield for the Calloways, and which fund pays more after tax?
o: 5.29%; the municipal fund
5.71%; the municipal fund
5.57%; the municipal fund
5.57%; the corporate fund
items.e: Double tax-exempt bond, itemizer: TEY = tax-free yield ÷ [(1 − state rate)(1 − federal rate)] = 3.6% ÷ (0.95 × 0.68) = 3.6% ÷ 0.646 = 5.57%. The 32% and 5% brackets are case assumptions (2026 edition figure). Since 5.57% > 5.2%, the municipal fund pays more after tax. Adding the brackets (3.6% ÷ 0.63 = 5.71%) applies only to non-itemizers.

items.q: Which change makes the Calloways' asset placement most tax-efficient while keeping their overall stock/bond mix?
o: Hold the taxable bond exposure in the 401(k) and keep tax-efficient index funds or municipals in the joint account
Buy municipal bonds inside Nadia’s Roth IRA so the bond income is doubly tax-free
Keep the bond fund in the joint account, since its interest is taxed the same in any account
Swap the bond fund for taxable zero-coupon corporate bonds in the joint account to defer the interest
items.e: Tax-inefficient holdings (taxable interest, nonqualified dividends, high turnover) are best kept in tax-deferred accounts; tax-efficient ones (broad index funds, qualified dividends, municipals) can sit in taxable accounts. Swapping bonds into the 401(k) and stocks into the joint account keeps the same mix while sheltering interest now taxed at 32% federal and 5% state (2026 edition figure).

items.q: Using the duration formula, approximately what will the Calloways' Ridgeway position be worth after the rate increase?
items.e: ΔP ÷ P = −D × [Δy ÷ (1 + y)] = −6.2 × (0.01 ÷ 1.052) = −5.89%. Change = −0.0589 × $60,000 ≈ −$3,536, so the value is about $56,464. The rule of thumb (6.2 × 1%) gives $56,280. A bond fund never matures, so this price risk cannot be removed by holding on.

items.q: Which fixed-income approach best protects the money for Leah's first tuition bill?
o: A long-term bond fund with a duration of 14, for its higher yield
Three-year Treasury zero-coupon bonds, whose duration equals the three-year horizon
A barbell of 1-year and 20-year bonds
Keep the stock index fund, since stocks beat bonds over long periods
items.e: Matching a portfolio’s duration to the time until the money is needed immunizes it: higher rates lower prices but raise reinvestment income, and vice versa. A zero-coupon bond’s duration equals its maturity, so a 3-year Treasury zero delivers a known sum on schedule with no default or reinvestment risk. In a taxable account the accrued interest is taxed yearly (phantom income).

items.q: What was the Calloways' holding period return on the Summit fund in U.S. dollars?
items.e: Convert at both ends: $36,000 ÷ 1.08 = €33,333; × 1.09 = €36,333; × $1.02 = $37,060. HPR = ($37,060 − $36,000) ÷ $36,000 = 2.94%, or 1.09 × (1.02 ÷ 1.08) − 1. The euro fell against the dollar, shrinking a 9% local gain to about 3%. A U.S. investor abroad wants the dollar to fall during the holding period.
